observations:
Torah #246 is a two-paragraph aphorism with a single, tightly unified conceptual axis. The source text yields exactly two connected components from explicit bechina-type language:

1. גַּדְלוּת ↔ תַּעֲנִית (Package 1, good): The Rebbe explicitly equates gadlut with a fast ('הוּא מוֹעִיל כְּמוֹ תַּעֲנִית'). These two concepts share one essential nature: voluntary self-emptying of prior wisdom to make room for a higher comprehension.

2. גַּאֲוָה ↔ שׁוֹטֶה (Package 2, evil): The Rebbe states that if one genuinely becomes proud, one becomes 'שׁוֹטֶה מַמָּשׁ' — an actual fool. These share the essential nature of the person whose wisdom has been extinguished.

All other concepts in the Torah (הַשָּׂגָה, מַדְרֵגָה, תּוֹרַת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, תַּלְמוּד בַּבְלִי, חָכְמָה יְתֵרָה, אָמָּנוּת יְתֵרָה, עָנָו) are either:
  - Eitza nodes (they are outcomes or prerequisites, not parallel-nature equivalences): hashagah is the goal that gadlut/ta'anit leads to; chokhmah yeteirah and amanut yeteirah are the prerequisites for practicing gadlut safely; being anav is the desired endpoint.
  - Contextual references (Talmud Bavli, Torat Eretz Yisrael) used as illustrative examples of the lower and higher wisdom in the Rabbi Zeira story.

None of these remaining concepts form a cluster of 3+ bechina-connected nodes that constitute an independent domain separate from the two existing packages. The Torah does not contain enough bechina language to generate additional packages. The teaching is deliberately compact — the Rebbe states a single equivalence (gadlut = ta'anit), warns against its evil twin (gaavah = shote), and leaves everything else to the practitioner's wisdom and artistry (chokhmah yeteirah, amanut yeteirah).

Conclusion: Two packages fully capture the conceptual structure of Torah #246. No new packages are proposed.
